item.description:
💗 A job offer mentions a “probation period.”
What does that mean?

A probation period is an initial stage of employment during which a company evaluates a new employee's performance, suitability for the role and how they're adapting to the team.

Depending on local employment laws and the contract, this period may involve specific performance reviews or different notice requirements.

But being on probation doesn't automatically mean an employee has no employment rights.

Before accepting a position, it's worth checking how long the probation period lasts, how performance will be evaluated and whether any employment conditions change during that time.

The rules vary by country, so understanding the terms of the agreement is important.

item.title: 💗 Do you need a portfolio if you're not a developer or designer? Not necessarily
item.description:
💗 Do you need a portfolio if you're not a developer or designer?

Not necessarily, but having examples of your work can help you stand out when applying for Web3 jobs.

And a portfolio doesn't have to be a fancy website!

Whether you work in marketing, community management, customer support, BD or operations, you can use a simple Notion page, Google Doc or PDF to showcase your experience.

What should you include?

• Projects or campaigns you've worked on
• Problems you've helped solve
• Your specific responsibilities and contributions
• Results, improvements or lessons learned

For each example, explain what the challenge was, what you did and what happened as a result.

You don't need impressive numbers or dozens of projects. A few clear examples can help hiring teams understand your experience better than a list of responsibilities alone.

Just make sure you're not sharing confidential information or private company data.

item.title: 🎉 Excited to announce that CryptoJobsList has acquired Crypto.Jobs 🤝 Both job bo
item.description:
🎉 Excited to announce that CryptoJobsList has acquired Crypto.Jobs 🤝

Both job boards started in 2017, back when crypto was small and getting a job in it was tough. Crypto.jobs went on to help more than 3,000 teams hire, including Consensys, CoinList and Parity.

Starting today, crypto.jobs redirects to CryptoJobsList, so there's one place for Web3 hiring. Every job is reviewed by a person before it goes live, and Crypto.jobs customers are moving over without any break in their hiring.

Crypto hiring has outgrown the scattered boards of the early days. Teams shouldn't have to run split hiring pipelines, and candidates shouldn't have to wonder whether a job post is real.

Thank you to the founder of Crypto.jobs for years of friendly competition and for making this handoff so smooth.

Read full announcement 👉 https://cryptojobslist.com/blog/cryptojobslist-acquires-crypto-jobs

ps.
🙏 Special thanks to the Founder of Crypto.jobs for years of friendly competition and a smooth transition.

item.title: 💗 Should you apply as soon as a job is posted? Sometimes, applying early can be
item.description:
💗 Should you apply as soon as a job is posted?

Sometimes, applying early can be helpful!

Some companies review applications as they arrive and begin interviewing before the position closes.

But not every hiring team works that way. Others review candidates in batches or wait until the application deadline.

🔜 So, what's the best strategy?

• Apply to relevant opportunities when you find them.
• Don't rush through your resume just to submit first.
• Pay attention to deadlines and whether applications are reviewed on a rolling basis.
• Don't automatically skip a job because it already has hundreds of applicants.

Being first doesn't guarantee an interview. Being applicant #200 doesn't automatically disqualify you either.

item.title: 💗 A recruiter asks you for professional references. What happens next? 👀 Some co
item.description:
💗 A recruiter asks you for professional references. What happens next? 👀

Some companies contact former managers or colleagues before making a hiring decision.

They're usually trying to understand what it was like to work with you, confirm aspects of your experience and learn more about how you handled responsibilities.

🔜 So, how should you prepare?

• Choose relevant references.
Someone who worked closely with you and can speak about your actual contributions is more useful than someone with an impressive title who barely knows your work.

• Ask for permission first.
Make sure they're comfortable being contacted and that their contact details are up to date.

• Give them context.
Let them know which role you're interviewing for and what responsibilities it involves.

• Protect your current position.
If you're employed and don't want your current manager contacted, communicate that clearly to the recruiter.

And remember, reference checks aren't always the final step. Some companies conduct them earlier, while others don't require them at all.

A good reference isn't necessarily the most senior person you've worked with. It's someone who can genuinely speak about your experience.

item.title: 💗 Does an ATS automatically reject your resume? You've probably seen claims that
item.description:
💗 Does an ATS automatically reject your resume?

You've probably seen claims that most resumes get rejected by an Applicant Tracking System before a recruiter even reads them.

But that's not how every ATS works.

An ATS is primarily a tool companies use to collect, organize and manage applications.

Some systems support automated screening based on employer-defined criteria, while others also offer AI-assisted features.

And here's something worth knowing: there's no universal ATS score or magic resume template that guarantees you'll pass.

So, what can you actually do?

• Keep your resume formatting simple and readable.
• Use relevant keywords naturally when they reflect your experience.
• Make sure your qualifications are clearly described.
• Answer application questions accurately.
• Follow the employer's submission instructions.

Your goal shouldn't be to beat an algorithm. It should be to make your experience easy to evaluate.
